title: The serenity prayer
hook: Reinhold Niebuhr is credited with the prayer asking serenity, courage and wisdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul Tillich and ultimate concern: faith as being grasped by what matters most. Your line was what matters most.

It hangs on kitchen walls. It's printed on mugs and bookmarks and tucked into wallets. Some people can say it by heart without remembering where they learned it. It's a short prayer, and its request is plain: serenity to accept the things that can't be changed, courage to change the things that can, and wisdom to know the difference. The prayer is credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, an American preacher and theologian, and it has traveled a long way from any one pulpit since.

Look at the shape of it. The first two requests pull in opposite directions. One says: let it go. The other says: get up and do something. A person can lean too far either way, fighting what will never move, or shrugging at what could be fixed by Thursday. The prayer won't pick a side. It asks for both, and then for the thing that decides between them. That last request is the hinge. The letter of James says: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him." Upbraideth not: in James's picture, God doesn't scold anyone for asking. The Gospels show both halves in a single night. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." He really asks, and he really yields. Paul tells a smaller story about a thorn in the flesh. He begged for it to be taken away, and the answer he heard was: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The letter never says the thorn left. When he is weak, Paul goes on, then he is strong. So the serenity prayer isn't a shrug. Its last line asks for judgment, fresh each time: is this a wall to accept, or a door to push? Some days the honest answer is, not sure yet. Which is exactly why the prayer asks for wisdom.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one situation that's been sitting on your chest, and sort it gently: set down the part you can't change, the past, another person's choices, and hold up the part you can, even a little, a phone call, an apology, a first step. If you pray, you can say the serenity prayer slowly, in the words you know, pausing after each line; if you don't, just let the sorting happen.
The serenity prayer. A short prayer credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, asking for serenity, for courage, and for the wisdom to tell which one this moment needs.
Your line: know the difference. Serenity, courage, and the wisdom between them. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray the serenity prayer daily or keep it on a wall at home; it is also said aloud together in some recovery groups and other gatherings.

fork.setup: you're Paul. something you call a thorn in the flesh won't go away. you've asked God to take it, and the answer is: my grace is sufficient for thee. what do you do?
options: accept it, and lean on that grace.
fork.reveal: Paul says he will glory in his weaknesses instead, because God's strength is made perfect in weakness.

original.note: Greek, James 1:5: wisdom. James says to ask God for it, who "upbraideth not."

chat.says: Isn't the serenity prayer just about accepting things and not making waves?
options: No. It also asks for courage to change what can be changed, and wisdom to tell which is which.
Yes. Its point is that most things can't be changed, so it's best to let them all go.
No. It's about pushing to change everything, since accepting anything is giving up.
chat.meaning: The prayer asks for serenity and for courage, which pull opposite ways, and then for the wisdom to know which one this moment needs.

notes: The prayer itself is not quoted: its wording is modern and its rights status is unclear. The hook and word paraphrase its three requests (serenity, courage, wisdom). The index hook's 'is credited to' is kept; authorship has been debated, so the script never says Niebuhr wrote it.
'An American preacher and theologian' for Niebuhr: confirm.
howItsDone says it is said 'in some recovery groups and other gatherings'; a soft claim, confirm acceptable.
'Paul kept traveling, writing and working anyway' is a summary of Paul's continuing ministry after 2 Corinthians 12, not a statement from that passage; confirm.

Editor pass: cut 'Paul kept traveling, writing and working anyway' (not in the cited passage); the teach, myth, fork and trapdoor now stay inside 2 Corinthians 12:7–10 (the thorn is never said to leave; 'when I am weak, then am I strong', paraphrased).
Practice outline says 'pray it'; written as 'if you pray, you can say the serenity prayer ... in the words you know', with a sorting exercise for those who don't pray.

Audit (2026-10-02): the line 'God doesn't scold you for asking' was the narrator speaking for God; now attributed to James. The trapdoor's third floor was a re-run of the teach (Gethsemane, the thorn) and now gives the authorship debate and the James 1:5 echo instead.
